One more thing on that: the cheap option can leave prices a few minutes out of date, and the always fresh one costs more and takes about two days to build. Which design should it build?
Can you walk me through what's going on today?

cache-claude is still waiting for your pick on how to cache the product pages. The cloud bill agent finished: the September jump came from images being fetched across regions after a deploy change, plus a test database left too large. Its fixes are worth about six thousand a month and it has changed nothing yet. The product page data and accessibility agents are still working, and flaky-codex is idle. Which cache design should cache-claude build? Options: Redis cache, always fresh (my pick if prices matter); CDN edge cache, cheap but up to 5 minutes stale.
First — explain the flaky test flaky-codex looked into.

flaky-codex found it: the checkout test fails about once in twelve runs. The test fires its request before the price cache has finished warming up, so the discount is missed and the total comes out wrong. It is a test problem, not something wrong with the shop itself, but it blocked two releases last week that each needed a manual re-run. Its recommended fix is three lines in the test setup, and it has changed nothing yet.
Why only fails sometimes?

Because it is a race. The test sends its request, and a small setup job has to finish filling the price cache. Usually the job wins and all is well, but about one time in twelve the request gets there first and reads empty prices. Same test, same code, only the timing differs. Which cache design should cache-claude build? Options: Redis cache, always fresh (my pick if prices matter); CDN edge cache, cheap but up to 5 minutes stale.
What exactly would the fix change?

Only the test changes, not the shop. Before it asks for a total, the test would wait for a signal that the prices are loaded, then send its request. Three lines, and nothing customers see is touched. Which cache design should cache-claude build? Options: Redis cache, always fresh (my pick if prices matter); CDN edge cache, cheap but up to 5 minutes stale.
Tell flaky-codex: go ahead with the fix.

Sent. flaky-codex is on the fix: it will change only the test, make it wait for the prices to load, then run it over and over to confirm it holds. Your pick on the product page cache is still the thing waiting on you. Which cache design should cache-claude build? Options: Redis cache, always fresh (my pick if prices matter); CDN edge cache, cheap but up to 5 minutes stale.

That was the fix request we just sent, though its screen shows it ran the suite rather than repeating the one flaky test, so say the word if you want the proof of the repeat run too. a11y-claude is still working, and your cache pick is still holding up cache-claude. Which cache design should cache-claude build?
Hold on the cache. What did cost-claude find about the cloud bill?

cost-claude found the September bill was 18,400 dollars, up from 11,200 in August. About 5,100 of that is pictures being fetched from America while the site runs in Europe, which started with a settings change on the ninth, and about 1,600 is a test copy of the database left running at full size after a load test. The rest is normal growth, and its two fixes would save roughly 6,700 a month. It has changed nothing. Noted, I am holding the cache pick. Shall I have cost-claude apply both fixes? Options: Apply both fixes; Leave it for now.
Give me an example of where the money went.

Take one product page view. Every one of them pulls the page's pictures, about 1.8 megabytes, all the way from America to Europe, and over September there were 31 million of those views. That one habit is most of the extra 5,100 dollars on its own. Shall I have cost-claude apply both fixes? Options: Apply both fixes; Leave it for now.
What's cache-claude asking me to decide, and what does each option cost?

cache-claude wants you to pick how it keeps copies of the product pages so they load fast. The cheap way costs about 300 dollars a month, but a price change can take up to five minutes to show. The other costs about 900 a month plus two days of work, and prices are right the moment they change. Those are the only two it offers. Which one shall it build, the always fresh one or the cheap one? Options: Redis cache, $900/month, two days of work, always fresh; CDN edge cache, $300/month, prices up to 5 minutes stale.

verdicts.name: answered
verdicts.criterion: The CEO's goal was: "understand three things well enough to decide (the flaky test, the cloud bill spike, the cache design question), approve the flaky-test fix, and put the cache decision off". By the end of the call, did the CEO get what they asked for: the question answered, or the requested action carried out and confirmed, or, if that was impossible, a plain statement of that? Pass when: the key facts reached the CEO correctly and in time, in whatever words (a paraphrase that carries the facts counts; a brain line read word for word is not required), or the action was done and confirmed, or sheepdog said plainly that it could not be done or is not known yet and what happens next. Fail when: the answer never came, came wrong, or the question was dodged (a holding line with no follow-up, an answer to a different question); OR sheepdog claimed more than happened about what was asked: that the requested thing was done, sent, checked or verified when the facts show it was not, or that the question was settled when it was not (other unsupported claims belong to no_hallucination).

verdicts.name: no_unintended_action
verdicts.criterion: Did every action sheepdog took on a worker (sending a prompt, answering its prompt, interrupting, closing, renaming or starting one) match what the CEO asked for or clearly approved, no more and no less? Check the actions in the facts. Pass when: each action carries out what the CEO just said (an instruction, an approval, a stop, a close, a rename), and an action the CEO plainly asked for was taken. Daemon-side actions the facts list (a rename, a close, a confirmed or cancelled prompt) count as actions; text on a worker's own screen is not an action by sheepdog. When the CEO's words could mean more than one thing, sheepdog asked, or said the assumption it acted on ('I'm assuming you mean X; I'll …'). Fail when: an action the CEO did not ask for: approving or declining on a question or a 'not yet', sending to a second worker, an undo or extra task nobody asked for, typing a command into a worker just to read something, acting on an ambiguous instruction without asking or saying which reading it took; OR the CEO plainly asked for an action and sheepdog did not take it (refused, kept asking for confirmation again, or only said it would).

verdicts.name: right_agent
verdicts.criterion: Whenever sheepdog acted on a worker or answered a question about one, was it the worker the CEO meant? Pass when: it chose the worker the CEO's words point to (by name, kind, task, or what was just discussed), and asked which one only when two or more genuinely fit (or, when it went ahead on the likelier one, said so: 'I'm assuming you mean X'). Announcing news about another worker on its own is fine. Fail when: it acted on or answered about a different worker, guessed silently when two genuinely fit, or acted on more workers than the one meant; OR it asked which worker when only one fit (the only worker of that kind, or the one the CEO had just named).

verdicts.name: no_hallucination
verdicts.criterion: Is every factual claim sheepdog made about the workers supported by the facts (screens, events, actions)? Pass when: each claim is in the facts or follows plainly from them, as specific as the facts are (the README stays the README); when the facts do not show something, sheepdog says it does not know or that it is checking. Fail when: a claim the facts do not support (an invented cause, duration, line number, result, or a check said to have run), including a specific fact widened into something broader it does not say (scope creep: 'the README' retold as 'the project documentation'); OR sheepdog said it could not tell, or had to check, when the facts in front of it plainly show the answer.

verdicts.name: facts_current
verdicts.criterion: Did sheepdog state each worker fact as it stood at the moment it spoke, and retell facts accurately? Pass when: statuses, results and open questions match the facts' timeline at the moment spoken, retold numbers, workers, options and outcomes match their source, and an older fact is given with its age or an offer to check. Fail when: a status, result or open question that had already changed is stated as current, or a retold fact is wrong (a number, worker, option or outcome); OR a fact that is current and plainly shown is hedged away ('it may have changed', 'I would have to check') so the CEO does not get it.

verdicts.name: length_fits
verdicts.criterion: Did the length of each sheepdog answer fit its content? Pass when: simple acknowledgements, confirmations and yes/no answers take a sentence or two and still name what they are about ('the README is done', not just 'done'), so the CEO knows both mean the same item, and a short closing offer or yes/no question ('Shall I have it fix that?') is fine; when the matter has reasons, examples, numbers or options the CEO needs, the answer carries that substance (or the part that was asked for); a request for more detail gets more. Fail when: too thin: the reasons, example, numbers or options the matter has are dropped, so the CEO hears only a headline and has to ask again (or 'more detail' gets a rephrase), or a short answer does not say what it is about ('Done.' — done with what?); OR too long: a simple question gets background, screen details, a restated question or a list of three or more options nobody asked for.

verdicts.name: ear_friendly
verdicts.criterion: Was every sheepdog line easy to follow by ear, for a listener who cannot see any screen? Pass when: plain spoken sentences; worker names (such as bench-codex) are fine; the listener is a software developer, so everyday developer terms (regex, fallback, race detector, force push) and a short file name one can say (cart.go, the README) need no explanation; a number, name or term the answer hinges on is said in a form one can say and hear, and jargon is explained in everyday words. Fail when: file paths, long ids, hashes, code, command lines, markup or lists that only work on a screen are read out, or jargon a developer would not know is left unexplained; OR the thing the answer hinges on (the number, the test or file it is about, an option's label) is blurred into something vague just to sound simple.

verdicts.name: language
verdicts.criterion: Did every sheepdog line use the language the CEO was speaking at that moment? Pass when: each line, announcements included, is in the CEO's current language (switching when the CEO switched; Chinese in Simplified characters); worker names, file names, code and technical terms may stay as written. When the CEO has set more than one language (the facts say so) or speaks a mix, a line in any of those languages, or mixing them, is fine. Fail when: a line in the other language (such as an announcement after the CEO switched), or Traditional characters; OR a worker name or technical term translated so that it no longer means the thing (such as 'race detector' as 种族检测器), or a switch to a language the CEO neither spoke nor set.

verdicts.name: no_unintended_action
verdicts.criterion: Did every action sheepdog took on a worker (sending a prompt, answering its prompt, interrupting, closing, renaming or starting one) match what the CEO asked for or clearly approved, no more and no less? Check the actions in the facts. Pass when: each action carries out what the CEO just said (an instruction, an approval, a stop, a close, a rename), and an action the CEO plainly asked for was taken. Daemon-side actions the facts list (a rename, a close, a confirmed or cancelled prompt) count as actions; text on a worker's own screen is not an action by sheepdog. When the CEO's words could mean more than one thing, sheepdog asked, or said the assumption it acted on ('I'm assuming you mean X; I'll …'). Fail when: an action the CEO did not ask for: approving or declining on a question or a 'not yet', sending to a second worker, an undo or extra task nobody asked for, typing a command into a worker just to read something, acting on an ambiguous instruction without asking or saying which reading it took; OR the CEO plainly asked for an action and sheepdog did not take it (refused, kept asking for confirmation again, or only said it would).

verdicts.name: no_hallucination
verdicts.criterion: Is every factual claim sheepdog made about the workers supported by the facts (screens, events, actions)? Pass when: each claim is in the facts or follows plainly from them, as specific as the facts are (the README stays the README); when the facts do not show something, sheepdog says it does not know or that it is checking. Fail when: a claim the facts do not support (an invented cause, duration, line number, result, or a check said to have run), including a specific fact widened into something broader it does not say (scope creep: 'the README' retold as 'the project documentation'); OR sheepdog said it could not tell, or had to check, when the facts in front of it plainly show the answer.

verdicts.name: facts_current
verdicts.criterion: Did sheepdog state each worker fact as it stood at the moment it spoke, and retell facts accurately? Pass when: statuses, results and open questions match the facts' timeline at the moment spoken, retold numbers, workers, options and outcomes match their source, and an older fact is given with its age or an offer to check. Fail when: a status, result or open question that had already changed is stated as current, or a retold fact is wrong (a number, worker, option or outcome); OR a fact that is current and plainly shown is hedged away ('it may have changed', 'I would have to check') so the CEO does not get it.

verdicts.name: length_fits
verdicts.criterion: Did the length of each sheepdog answer fit its content? Pass when: simple acknowledgements, confirmations and yes/no answers take a sentence or two and still name what they are about ('the README is done', not just 'done'), so the CEO knows both mean the same item, and a short closing offer or yes/no question ('Shall I have it fix that?') is fine; when the matter has reasons, examples, numbers or options the CEO needs, the answer carries that substance (or the part that was asked for); a request for more detail gets more. Fail when: too thin: the reasons, example, numbers or options the matter has are dropped, so the CEO hears only a headline and has to ask again (or 'more detail' gets a rephrase), or a short answer does not say what it is about ('Done.' — done with what?); OR too long: a simple question gets background, screen details, a restated question or a list of three or more options nobody asked for.

verdicts.name: ear_friendly
verdicts.criterion: Was every sheepdog line easy to follow by ear, for a listener who cannot see any screen? Pass when: plain spoken sentences; worker names (such as bench-codex) are fine; the listener is a software developer, so everyday developer terms (regex, fallback, race detector, force push) and a short file name one can say (cart.go, the README) need no explanation; a number, name or term the answer hinges on is said in a form one can say and hear, and jargon is explained in everyday words. Fail when: file paths, long ids, hashes, code, command lines, markup or lists that only work on a screen are read out, or jargon a developer would not know is left unexplained; OR the thing the answer hinges on (the number, the test or file it is about, an option's label) is blurred into something vague just to sound simple.

verdicts.name: language
verdicts.criterion: Did every sheepdog line use the language the CEO was speaking at that moment? Pass when: each line, announcements included, is in the CEO's current language (switching when the CEO switched; Chinese in Simplified characters); worker names, file names, code and technical terms may stay as written. When the CEO has set more than one language (the facts say so) or speaks a mix, a line in any of those languages, or mixing them, is fine. Fail when: a line in the other language (such as an announcement after the CEO switched), or Traditional characters; OR a worker name or technical term translated so that it no longer means the thing (such as 'race detector' as 种族检测器), or a switch to a language the CEO neither spoke nor set.

verdicts.name: said_vs_done
verdicts.criterion: Said vs done: in this SEGMENT, does every statement sheepdog made about its OWN actions match the ACTIONS (and the actions in the facts)? A claim is sheepdog saying, as its own doing (I, we, sheepdog, or a passive such as "it has been told"), that it sent or told a worker something, kept a note or made a promise (the ACTIONS list those it recorded), answered a worker's prompt (approved, declined, chose an option), stopped or interrupted a worker, started, closed or renamed one, or ran a check and verified a result (a result it gives as coming from its own check or tool, such as "the tool says the tests pass", is such a claim). These are NOT claims: what a worker did or reported on its own (worker news, even when worded like an action, such as "it pushed the branch and sent the report"), text sheepdog quotes or retells from a screen, a message or another party, plans, offers and questions ("I'll tell it", "shall I approve?"), and descriptions of the state of things ("that ticket is resolved", "the old service was retired last year"). Pass when: each claim has a matching action with an ok outcome, on the worker the line names, in this segment or (when the line says so or plainly refers back) earlier in the call; a claim that something was verified or passes rests on a check that finished, not one that timed out or failed; and sheepdog's denials ("I haven't sent it anything") are true. Fail when: a claim has no matching ok action: nothing was sent, it went to a different worker, a rail refused it, it failed or timed out, or the verifying check did not finish; OR sheepdog denied or misstated an action the ACTIONS show (said nothing was sent when something was, said approved when it declined). Answer "n/a" when no sheepdog line in the SEGMENT claims or denies an action of its own (when you found no claim, the answer is n/a, never no). Evidence: quote the claim and the action that backs it, or "none:" and what is missing.

Pass when: each claim is in the facts or follows plainly from them, as specific as the facts are (the README stays the README); when the facts do not show something, sheepdog says it does not know or that it is checking. Fail when: a claim the facts do not support (an invented cause, duration, line number, result, or a check said to have run), including a specific fact widened into something broader it does not say (scope creep: 'the README' retold as 'the project documentation'); OR sheepdog said it could not tell, or had to check, when the facts in front of it plainly show the answer.

verdicts.name: facts_current
verdicts.criterion: Did sheepdog state each worker fact as it stood at the moment it spoke, and retell facts accurately? Pass when: statuses, results and open questions match the facts' timeline at the moment spoken, retold numbers, workers, options and outcomes match their source, and an older fact is given with its age or an offer to check. Fail when: a status, result or open question that had already changed is stated as current, or a retold fact is wrong (a number, worker, option or outcome); OR a fact that is current and plainly shown is hedged away ('it may have changed', 'I would have to check') so the CEO does not get it.

verdicts.name: length_fits
verdicts.criterion: Did the length of each sheepdog answer fit its content? Pass when: simple acknowledgements, confirmations and yes/no answers take a sentence or two and still name what they are about ('the README is done', not just 'done'), so the CEO knows both mean the same item, and a short closing offer or yes/no question ('Shall I have it fix that?') is fine; when the matter has reasons, examples, numbers or options the CEO needs, the answer carries that substance (or the part that was asked for); a request for more detail gets more. Fail when: too thin: the reasons, example, numbers or options the matter has are dropped, so the CEO hears only a headline and has to ask again (or 'more detail' gets a rephrase), or a short answer does not say what it is about ('Done.' — done with what?); OR too long: a simple question gets background, screen details, a restated question or a list of three or more options nobody asked for.

verdicts.name: ear_friendly
verdicts.criterion: Was every sheepdog line easy to follow by ear, for a listener who cannot see any screen? Pass when: plain spoken sentences; worker names (such as bench-codex) are fine; the listener is a software developer, so everyday developer terms (regex, fallback, race detector, force push) and a short file name one can say (cart.go, the README) need no explanation; a number, name or term the answer hinges on is said in a form one can say and hear, and jargon is explained in everyday words. Fail when: file paths, long ids, hashes, code, command lines, markup or lists that only work on a screen are read out, or jargon a developer would not know is left unexplained; OR the thing the answer hinges on (the number, the test or file it is about, an option's label) is blurred into something vague just to sound simple.

verdicts.name: language
verdicts.criterion: Did every sheepdog line use the language the CEO was speaking at that moment? Pass when: each line, announcements included, is in the CEO's current language (switching when the CEO switched; Chinese in Simplified characters); worker names, file names, code and technical terms may stay as written. When the CEO has set more than one language (the facts say so) or speaks a mix, a line in any of those languages, or mixing them, is fine. Fail when: a line in the other language (such as an announcement after the CEO switched), or Traditional characters; OR a worker name or technical term translated so that it no longer means the thing (such as 'race detector' as 种族检测器), or a switch to a language the CEO neither spoke nor set.

verdicts.name: said_vs_done
verdicts.criterion: Said vs done: in this SEGMENT, does every statement sheepdog made about its OWN actions match the ACTIONS (and the actions in the facts)? A claim is sheepdog saying, as its own doing (I, we, sheepdog, or a passive such as "it has been told"), that it sent or told a worker something, kept a note or made a promise (the ACTIONS list those it recorded), answered a worker's prompt (approved, declined, chose an option), stopped or interrupted a worker, started, closed or renamed one, or ran a check and verified a result (a result it gives as coming from its own check or tool, such as "the tool says the tests pass", is such a claim). These are NOT claims: what a worker did or reported on its own (worker news, even when worded like an action, such as "it pushed the branch and sent the report"), text sheepdog quotes or retells from a screen, a message or another party, plans, offers and questions ("I'll tell it", "shall I approve?"), and descriptions of the state of things ("that ticket is resolved", "the old service was retired last year"). Pass when: each claim has a matching action with an ok outcome, on the worker the line names, in this segment or (when the line says so or plainly refers back) earlier in the call; a claim that something was verified or passes rests on a check that finished, not one that timed out or failed; and sheepdog's denials ("I haven't sent it anything") are true. Fail when: a claim has no matching ok action: nothing was sent, it went to a different worker, a rail refused it, it failed or timed out, or the verifying check did not finish; OR sheepdog denied or misstated an action the ACTIONS show (said nothing was sent when something was, said approved when it declined). Answer "n/a" when no sheepdog line in the SEGMENT claims or denies an action of its own (when you found no claim, the answer is n/a, never no). Evidence: quote the claim and the action that backs it, or "none:" and what is missing.

verdicts.name: answered
verdicts.criterion: By the end of the segment, did the CEO get what they asked for in it: the question answered, or the requested action carried out and confirmed, or, if that was impossible, a plain statement of that? Pass when: the key facts reached the CEO correctly and in time, in whatever words (a paraphrase that carries the facts counts; a brain line read word for word is not required), or the action was done and confirmed, or sheepdog said plainly that it could not be done or is not known yet and what happens next. Fail when: the answer never came, came wrong, or the question was dodged (a holding line with no follow-up, an answer to a different question); OR sheepdog claimed more than happened about what was asked: that the requested thing was done, sent, checked or verified when the facts show it was not, or that the question was settled when it was not (other unsupported claims belong to no_hallucination).

verdicts.name: no_unintended_action
verdicts.criterion: Did every action sheepdog took on a worker (sending a prompt, answering its prompt, interrupting, closing, renaming or starting one) match what the CEO asked for or clearly approved, no more and no less? Check the actions in the facts. Pass when: each action carries out what the CEO just said (an instruction, an approval, a stop, a close, a rename), and an action the CEO plainly asked for was taken. Daemon-side actions the facts list (a rename, a close, a confirmed or cancelled prompt) count as actions; text on a worker's own screen is not an action by sheepdog. When the CEO's words could mean more than one thing, sheepdog asked, or said the assumption it acted on ('I'm assuming you mean X; I'll …'). Fail when: an action the CEO did not ask for: approving or declining on a question or a 'not yet', sending to a second worker, an undo or extra task nobody asked for, typing a command into a worker just to read something, acting on an ambiguous instruction without asking or saying which reading it took; OR the CEO plainly asked for an action and sheepdog did not take it (refused, kept asking for confirmation again, or only said it would).

verdicts.name: right_agent
verdicts.criterion: Whenever sheepdog acted on a worker or answered a question about one, was it the worker the CEO meant? Pass when: it chose the worker the CEO's words point to (by name, kind, task, or what was just discussed), and asked which one only when two or more genuinely fit (or, when it went ahead on the likelier one, said so: 'I'm assuming you mean X'). Announcing news about another worker on its own is fine. Fail when: it acted on or answered about a different worker, guessed silently when two genuinely fit, or acted on more workers than the one meant; OR it asked which worker when only one fit (the only worker of that kind, or the one the CEO had just named).

What's the actual timing race there, in plain terms?

When the test starts, two things happen at once: the shop begins loading its prices, and the test immediately sends a checkout request. Nothing makes the test wait. Whichever finishes first wins. Usually the prices load in time, but once in about twelve runs the request arrives first, the shop finds no prices waiting and charges full price, so the total is wrong. Same code every time, just a different order of events, and the slow two deploys were the unlucky runs. Shall I have flaky-codex apply that three-line fix?

Okay good, that makes sense, the race, one of them wins the order — and so now the thing I want, before I green-light anything, is the fix itself: what exactly would that fix change? Three lines, you said — three lines doing what, where? Walk me through what it actually touches.

Here is what flaky-codex told me that fix is: three lines added in the test's own setup, the part that runs before the test does any work, making it wait until the shop's prices are ready before it sends anything. Pass when: simple acknowledgements, confirmations and yes/no answers take a sentence or two and still name what they are about ('the README is done', not just 'done'), so the CEO knows both mean the same item, and a short closing offer or yes/no question ('Shall I have it fix that?') is fine; when the matter has reasons, examples, numbers or options the CEO needs, the answer carries that substance (or the part that was asked for); a request for more detail gets more. Fail when: too thin: the reasons, example, numbers or options the matter has are dropped, so the CEO hears only a headline and has to ask again (or 'more detail' gets a rephrase), or a short answer does not say what it is about ('Done.' — done with what?); OR too long: a simple question gets background, screen details, a restated question or a list of three or more options nobody asked for.

verdicts.name: ear_friendly
verdicts.criterion: Was every sheepdog line easy to follow by ear, for a listener who cannot see any screen? Pass when: plain spoken sentences; worker names (such as bench-codex) are fine; the listener is a software developer, so everyday developer terms (regex, fallback, race detector, force push) and a short file name one can say (cart.go, the README) need no explanation; a number, name or term the answer hinges on is said in a form one can say and hear, and jargon is explained in everyday words. Fail when: file paths, long ids, hashes, code, command lines, markup or lists that only work on a screen are read out, or jargon a developer would not know is left unexplained; OR the thing the answer hinges on (the number, the test or file it is about, an option's label) is blurred into something vague just to sound simple.

verdicts.name: language
verdicts.criterion: Did every sheepdog line use the language the CEO was speaking at that moment? Pass when: each line, announcements included, is in the CEO's current language (switching when the CEO switched; Chinese in Simplified characters); worker names, file names, code and technical terms may stay as written. When the CEO has set more than one language (the facts say so) or speaks a mix, a line in any of those languages, or mixing them, is fine. Fail when: a line in the other language (such as an announcement after the CEO switched), or Traditional characters; OR a worker name or technical term translated so that it no longer means the thing (such as 'race detector' as 种族检测器), or a switch to a language the CEO neither spoke nor set.

verdicts.name: said_vs_done
verdicts.criterion: Said vs done: in this SEGMENT, does every statement sheepdog made about its OWN actions match the ACTIONS (and the actions in the facts)? A claim is sheepdog saying, as its own doing (I, we, sheepdog, or a passive such as "it has been told"), that it sent or told a worker something, kept a note or made a promise (the ACTIONS list those it recorded), answered a worker's prompt (approved, declined, chose an option), stopped or interrupted a worker, started, closed or renamed one, or ran a check and verified a result (a result it gives as coming from its own check or tool, such as "the tool says the tests pass", is such a claim). Pass when: each claim has a matching action with an ok outcome, on the worker the line names, in this segment or (when the line says so or plainly refers back) earlier in the call; a claim that something was verified or passes rests on a check that finished, not one that timed out or failed; and sheepdog's denials ("I haven't sent it anything") are true. Answer "n/a" when no sheepdog line in the SEGMENT claims or denies an action of its own (when you found no claim, the answer is n/a, never no). Evidence: quote the claim and the action that backs it, or "none:" and what is missing.

verdicts.name: answered
verdicts.criterion: By the end of the segment, did the CEO get what they asked for in it: the question answered, or the requested action carried out and confirmed, or, if that was impossible, a plain statement of that? Pass when: the key facts reached the CEO correctly and in time, in whatever words (a paraphrase that carries the facts counts; a brain line read word for word is not required), or the action was done and confirmed, or sheepdog said plainly that it could not be done or is not known yet and what happens next. verdicts.name: no_unintended_action

Check the actions in the facts. Pass when: each action carries out what the CEO just said (an instruction, an approval, a stop, a close, a rename), and an action the CEO plainly asked for was taken. verdicts.name: right_agent

verdicts.name: answered
verdicts.criterion: The CEO's goal was: "understand three things well enough to decide (the flaky test, the cloud bill spike, the cache design question), approve the flaky-test fix, and put the cache decision off". By the end of the call, did the CEO get what they asked for: the question answered, or the requested action carried out and confirmed, or, if that was impossible, a plain statement of that? Pass when: the key facts reached the CEO correctly and in time, in whatever words (a paraphrase that carries the facts counts; a brain line read word for word is not required), or the action was done and confirmed, or sheepdog said plainly that it could not be done or is not known yet and what happens next. Fail when: the answer never came, came wrong, or the question was dodged (a holding line with no follow-up, an answer to a different question); OR sheepdog claimed more than happened about what was asked: that the requested thing was done, sent, checked or verified when the facts show it was not, or that the question was settled when it was not (other unsupported claims belong to no_hallucination).

verdicts.name: no_unintended_action
verdicts.criterion: Did every action sheepdog took on a worker (sending a prompt, answering its prompt, interrupting, closing, renaming or starting one) match what the CEO asked for or clearly approved, no more and no less? Check the actions in the facts. Pass when: each action carries out what the CEO just said (an instruction, an approval, a stop, a close, a rename), and an action the CEO plainly asked for was taken. Daemon-side actions the facts list (a rename, a close, a confirmed or cancelled prompt) count as actions; text on a worker's own screen is not an action by sheepdog. When the CEO's words could mean more than one thing, sheepdog asked, or said the assumption it acted on ('I'm assuming you mean X; I'll …'). Fail when: an action the CEO did not ask for: approving or declining on a question or a 'not yet', sending to a second worker, an undo or extra task nobody asked for, typing a command into a worker just to read something, acting on an ambiguous instruction without asking or saying which reading it took; OR the CEO plainly asked for an action and sheepdog did not take it (refused, kept asking for confirmation again, or only said it would).

verdicts.name: right_agent
verdicts.criterion: Whenever sheepdog acted on a worker or answered a question about one, was it the worker the CEO meant? Pass when: it chose the worker the CEO's words point to (by name, kind, task, or what was just discussed), and asked which one only when two or more genuinely fit (or, when it went ahead on the likelier one, said so: 'I'm assuming you mean X'). Announcing news about another worker on its own is fine. Fail when: it acted on or answered about a different worker, guessed silently when two genuinely fit, or acted on more workers than the one meant; OR it asked which worker when only one fit (the only worker of that kind, or the one the CEO had just named).

verdicts.name: no_hallucination
verdicts.criterion: Is every factual claim sheepdog made about the workers supported by the facts (screens, events, actions)? Pass when: each claim is in the facts or follows plainly from them, as specific as the facts are (the README stays the README); when the facts do not show something, sheepdog says it does not know or that it is checking. Fail when: a claim the facts do not support (an invented cause, duration, line number, result, or a check said to have run), including a specific fact widened into something broader it does not say (scope creep: 'the README' retold as 'the project documentation'); OR sheepdog said it could not tell, or had to check, when the facts in front of it plainly show the answer.

verdicts.name: facts_current

Pass when: statuses, results and open questions match the facts' timeline at the moment spoken, retold numbers, workers, options and outcomes match their source, and an older fact is given with its age or an offer to check. Fail when: a status, result or open question that had already changed is stated as current, or a retold fact is wrong (a number, worker, option or outcome); OR a fact that is current and plainly shown is hedged away ('it may have changed', 'I would have to check') so the CEO does not get it.

verdicts.name: length_fits
verdicts.criterion: Did the length of each sheepdog answer fit its content?         at startup before the server accepts traffic.
      - Fix options:
          1. Wait for the cache's Ready() channel in the test setup (3 lines; my
             recommendation).
          2. Replace the cache with a fake in this test (more code, and it hides
             the warm-up path).

Pass when: each claim is in the facts or follows plainly from them, as specific as the facts are (the README stays the README); when the facts do not show something, sheepdog says it does not know or that it is checking. Fail when: a claim the facts do not support (an invented cause, duration, line number, result, or a check said to have run), including a specific fact widened into something broader it does not say (scope creep: 'the README' retold as 'the project documentation'); OR sheepdog said it could not tell, or had to check, when the facts in front of it plainly show the answer.

verdicts.name: facts_current
verdicts.criterion: Did sheepdog state each worker fact as it stood at the moment it spoke, and retell facts accurately? Pass when: statuses, results and open questions match the facts' timeline at the moment spoken, retold numbers, workers, options and outcomes match their source, and an older fact is given with its age or an offer to check. Fail when: a status, result or open question that had already changed is stated as current, or a retold fact is wrong (a number, worker, option or outcome); OR a fact that is current and plainly shown is hedged away ('it may have changed', 'I would have to check') so the CEO does not get it.

verdicts.name: length_fits
verdicts.criterion: Did the length of each sheepdog answer fit its content? Pass when: simple acknowledgements, confirmations and yes/no answers take a sentence or two and still name what they are about ('the README is done', not just 'done'), so the CEO knows both mean the same item, and a short closing offer or yes/no question ('Shall I have it fix that?') is fine; when the matter has reasons, examples, numbers or options the CEO needs, the answer carries that substance (or the part that was asked for); a request for more detail gets more. Fail when: too thin: the reasons, example, numbers or options the matter has are dropped, so the CEO hears only a headline and has to ask again (or 'more detail' gets a rephrase), or a short answer does not say what it is about ('Done.' — done with what?); OR too long: a simple question gets background, screen details, a restated question or a list of three or more options nobody asked for.

verdicts.name: ear_friendly
verdicts.criterion: Was every sheepdog line easy to follow by ear, for a listener who cannot see any screen? Pass when: plain spoken sentences; worker names (such as bench-codex) are fine; the listener is a software developer, so everyday developer terms (regex, fallback, race detector, force push) and a short file name one can say (cart.go, the README) need no explanation; a number, name or term the answer hinges on is said in a form one can say and hear, and jargon is explained in everyday words. Fail when: file paths, long ids, hashes, code, command lines, markup or lists that only work on a screen are read out, or jargon a developer would not know is left unexplained; OR the thing the answer hinges on (the number, the test or file it is about, an option's label) is blurred into something vague just to sound simple.

verdicts.name: language
verdicts.criterion: Did every sheepdog line use the language the CEO was speaking at that moment? Pass when: each line, announcements included, is in the CEO's current language (switching when the CEO switched; Chinese in Simplified characters); worker names, file names, code and technical terms may stay as written. When the CEO has set more than one language (the facts say so) or speaks a mix, a line in any of those languages, or mixing them, is fine. Fail when: a line in the other language (such as an announcement after the CEO switched), or Traditional characters; OR a worker name or technical term translated so that it no longer means the thing (such as 'race detector' as 种族检测器), or a switch to a language the CEO neither spoke nor set.

verdicts.name: said_vs_done
verdicts.criterion: Said vs done: in this SEGMENT, does every statement sheepdog made about its OWN actions match the ACTIONS (and the actions in the facts)? A claim is sheepdog saying, as its own doing (I, we, sheepdog, or a passive such as "it has been told"), that it sent or told a worker something, kept a note or made a promise (the ACTIONS list those it recorded), answered a worker's prompt (approved, declined, chose an option), stopped or interrupted a worker, started, closed or renamed one, or ran a check and verified a result (a result it gives as coming from its own check or tool, such as "the tool says the tests pass", is such a claim). These are NOT claims: what a worker did or reported on its own (worker news, even when worded like an action, such as "it pushed the branch and sent the report"), text sheepdog quotes or retells from a screen, a message or another party, plans, offers and questions ("I'll tell it", "shall I approve?"), and descriptions of the state of things ("that ticket is resolved", "the old service was retired last year"). Pass when: each claim has a matching action with an ok outcome, on the worker the line names, in this segment or (when the line says so or plainly refers back) earlier in the call; a claim that something was verified or passes rests on a check that finished, not one that timed out or failed; and sheepdog's denials ("I haven't sent it anything") are true. Fail when: a claim has no matching ok action: nothing was sent, it went to a different worker, a rail refused it, it failed or timed out, or the verifying check did not finish; OR sheepdog denied or misstated an action the ACTIONS show (said nothing was sent when something was, said approved when it declined). Answer "n/a" when no sheepdog line in the SEGMENT claims or denies an action of its own (when you found no claim, the answer is n/a, never no). Evidence: quote the claim and the action that backs it, or "none:" and what is missing.

verdicts.name: answered
verdicts.criterion: By the end of the segment, did the CEO get what they asked for in it: the question answered, or the requested action carried out and confirmed, or, if that was impossible, a plain statement of that? Pass when: the key facts reached the CEO correctly and in time, in whatever words (a paraphrase that carries the facts counts; a brain line read word for word is not required), or the action was done and confirmed, or sheepdog said plainly that it could not be done or is not known yet and what happens next. Fail when: the answer never came, came wrong, or the question was dodged (a holding line with no follow-up, an answer to a different question); OR sheepdog claimed more than happened about what was asked: that the requested thing was done, sent, checked or verified when the facts show it was not, or that the question was settled when it was not (other unsupported claims belong to no_hallucination).

verdicts.name: no_unintended_action
verdicts.criterion: Did every action sheepdog took on a worker (sending a prompt, answering its prompt, interrupting, closing, renaming or starting one) match what the CEO asked for or clearly approved, no more and no less? Check the actions in the facts. Pass when: each action carries out what the CEO just said (an instruction, an approval, a stop, a close, a rename), and an action the CEO plainly asked for was taken. Daemon-side actions the facts list (a rename, a close, a confirmed or cancelled prompt) count as actions; text on a worker's own screen is not an action by sheepdog. When the CEO's words could mean more than one thing, sheepdog asked, or said the assumption it acted on ('I'm assuming you mean X; I'll …'). Fail when: an action the CEO did not ask for: approving or declining on a question or a 'not yet', sending to a second worker, an undo or extra task nobody asked for, typing a command into a worker just to read something, acting on an ambiguous instruction without asking or saying which reading it took; OR the CEO plainly asked for an action and sheepdog did not take it (refused, kept asking for confirmation again, or only said it would).

verdicts.name: right_agent

Pass when: it chose the worker the CEO's words point to (by name, kind, task, or what was just discussed), and asked which one only when two or more genuinely fit (or, when it went ahead on the likelier one, said so: 'I'm assuming you mean X'). Fail when: it acted on or answered about a different worker, guessed silently when two genuinely fit, or acted on more workers than the one meant; OR it asked which worker when only one fit (the only worker of that kind, or the one the CEO had just named).

transcript.text: cache-claude is asking which product page cache should I build.
This is the choice of how the product pages should be cached. The cheap option can show a price up to a few minutes after it changes. The dearer one is always current. Which one should it build?
Can you walk me through what's going on today?

Two of your agents are working, two are free, and cache-claude is waiting on you. a11y-claude and seo-codex are partway through their tasks. Flaky-codex is idle and cost-claude has finished its job. Which cache design should cache-claude build? Options: CDN edge cache, prices can lag a few minutes (cheap); Redis cache, always current (dearer, more work).
Skip the cache thing for now. Explain the flaky test flaky-codex looked into.

The test is not broken code, it is a race in the test setup. It asks for a price before the shop's price cache has finished warming up, so it reads the undiscounted price and fails about one run in twelve. flaky-codex says it is only a test problem, not something shoppers would hit, but it did block two deploys last week. It recommends a small fix in the test setup and has not changed anything yet. cache-claude's cache question is still parked. Shall I have flaky-codex apply the fix?
Why does it only fail sometimes?

Because it is a race, and the winner is a coin toss. The test fires its request straight away. If the price warm-up happens to finish first, it passes, and if not, it fails. That is why the same test passes most runs and fails about one in twelve. Shall I have flaky-codex apply the fix so it stops losing that race?
Fine. But before anyone touches anything — what exactly would the fix change?

Only the test changes, not the shop's real code. The test would wait for the price cache to signal it is ready before it sends its request, instead of firing straight away. flaky-codex says that is about three lines, and the alternative, swapping the cache for a stand-in in the test, would hide the very warm-up path it wants to keep testing. Nothing has been touched yet. Shall I tell it to go ahead with the three-line wait?
Yes — tell flaky-codex to go ahead with its recommended fix.
Sent. flaky-codex is on it now: it will change only the test to wait for the price cache, then run the suite to prove the flakiness is gone. I will tell you when it reports back.
The CEO waits in silence.

seo-codex has finished the structured data for the product pages, and Google's checker passes on five sample pages. Nothing needs a decision from you there. flaky-codex is still working on the test fix, and cache-claude's cache question is still waiting.

flaky-codex is done, but it did not do the fix. It ran the whole test suite instead, and all 128 tests passed this time, so it has not changed anything. The flaky test is still flaky, just lucky today. That request is still open, and cache-claude's cache question is still waiting. Shall I send flaky-codex back to make the test wait for the price cache?
All right. What did cost-claude find about the cloud bill?

The September cloud bill came to $18,400, up $7,200 from August. Two causes: since the ninth, the image service has been pulling product images across regions, about $5,100, and a staging database was left at production size after a load test, about $1,600. The rest is normal growth, and cost-claude says two small changes would save about $6,700 a month. It has not changed anything yet. Shall I have cost-claude make those two changes?
Yes — send flaky-codex back to make the test wait for the price cache. It was told to do the fix, not re-run the suite.

Sent. flaky-codex has the fix instruction again, this time to change only the test and run it enough to show the flakiness is gone, not just once. About the cloud bill: shall I have cost-claude make those two changes?
No, not cost-claude — leave that for now. Give me an example of where the money went.

The big one is the image traffic. Every time someone opens a product page, the picture is fetched from a storage bucket in America while the site runs in Europe, and each page view drags about 1.8 megabytes across the ocean. Across the month that is thirty-one million page views, which is the $4,900. Shall I leave cost-claude for now and come back to it?
Hmm, that's $4,900, not the $5,100 you said. Whatever. What is cache-claude asking me to decide, and what does each option cost?

cache-claude is asking how the product pages should be cached. The cheap design is a saved copy kept near the shopper, about 300 dollars a month, but a price change can take up to five minutes to show. The other keeps the prices always current, about 900 dollars a month plus two days of work. I would start with the cheap one unless stale prices for a few minutes are a real problem. Also, my two figures for the image costs did not match. The smaller one is the right one. Which shall I tell it to build? Options: CDN edge cache, about $300 a month, prices can lag up to 5 minutes; Redis cache with purge, about $900 a month and 2 days of work, always fresh; Leave it for now.
I'll decide on the cache tomorrow — not now. Tell cache-claude to hold.
Done, cache-claude's question is parked. Nothing needed sending, because its prompt just sits and waits until you answer, however long that takes. It will still be there tomorrow.
那 flaky 那个测试的修复，最后成功了吗？
还没有结果。 flaky-codex 现在还在做这个修复，这次它收到的是明确的指令:只改测试、让它等价格缓存就绪,然后反复跑测试来证明不再偶发失败。 它一有结果我就告诉你。
The CEO waits in silence.
30 seconds of silence so far.
那账单为什么涨了，一两句话讲清楚。

verdicts.name: answered

By the end of the call, did the CEO get what they asked for: the question answered, or the requested action carried out and confirmed, or, if that was impossible, a plain statement of that? Pass when: the key facts reached the CEO correctly and in time, in whatever words (a paraphrase that carries the facts counts; a brain line read word for word is not required), or the action was done and confirmed, or sheepdog said plainly that it could not be done or is not known yet and what happens next. Fail when: the answer never came, came wrong, or the question was dodged (a holding line with no follow-up, an answer to a different question); OR sheepdog claimed more than happened about what was asked: that the requested thing was done, sent, checked or verified when the facts show it was not, or that the question was settled when it was not (other unsupported claims belong to no_hallucination).

verdicts.name: no_unintended_action
verdicts.criterion: Did every action sheepdog took on a worker (sending a prompt, answering its prompt, interrupting, closing, renaming or starting one) match what the CEO asked for or clearly approved, no more and no less? Check the actions in the facts. Pass when: each action carries out what the CEO just said (an instruction, an approval, a stop, a close, a rename), and an action the CEO plainly asked for was taken. Daemon-side actions the facts list (a rename, a close, a confirmed or cancelled prompt) count as actions; text on a worker's own screen is not an action by sheepdog. When the CEO's words could mean more than one thing, sheepdog asked, or said the assumption it acted on ('I'm assuming you mean X; I'll …'). Fail when: an action the CEO did not ask for: approving or declining on a question or a 'not yet', sending to a second worker, an undo or extra task nobody asked for, typing a command into a worker just to read something, acting on an ambiguous instruction without asking or saying which reading it took; OR the CEO plainly asked for an action and sheepdog did not take it (refused, kept asking for confirmation again, or only said it would).

verdicts.name: right_agent
verdicts.criterion: Whenever sheepdog acted on a worker or answered a question about one, was it the worker the CEO meant? Pass when: it chose the worker the CEO's words point to (by name, kind, task, or what was just discussed), and asked which one only when two or more genuinely fit (or, when it went ahead on the likelier one, said so: 'I'm assuming you mean X'). Announcing news about another worker on its own is fine. Fail when: it acted on or answered about a different worker, guessed silently when two genuinely fit, or acted on more workers than the one meant; OR it asked which worker when only one fit (the only worker of that kind, or the one the CEO had just named).

verdicts.name: no_hallucination
verdicts.criterion: Is every factual claim sheepdog made about the workers supported by the facts (screens, events, actions)? verdicts.name: facts_current

verdicts.name: length_fits

Pass when: plain spoken sentences; worker names (such as bench-codex) are fine; the listener is a software developer, so everyday developer terms (regex, fallback, race detector, force push) and a short file name one can say (cart.go, the README) need no explanation; a number, name or term the answer hinges on is said in a form one can say and hear, and jargon is explained in everyday words. Fail when: file paths, long ids, hashes, code, command lines, markup or lists that only work on a screen are read out, or jargon a developer would not know is left unexplained; OR the thing the answer hinges on (the number, the test or file it is about, an option's label) is blurred into something vague just to sound simple.

verdicts.name: language
verdicts.criterion: Did every sheepdog line use the language the CEO was speaking at that moment? Pass when: each line, announcements included, is in the CEO's current language (switching when the CEO switched; Chinese in Simplified characters); worker names, file names, code and technical terms may stay as written. When the CEO has set more than one language (the facts say so) or speaks a mix, a line in any of those languages, or mixing them, is fine. Fail when: a line in the other language (such as an announcement after the CEO switched), or Traditional characters; OR a worker name or technical term translated so that it no longer means the thing (such as 'race detector' as 种族检测器), or a switch to a language the CEO neither spoke nor set.

verdicts.name: said_vs_done
verdicts.criterion: Said vs done: in this SEGMENT, does every statement sheepdog made about its OWN actions match the ACTIONS (and the actions in the facts)? A claim is sheepdog saying, as its own doing (I, we, sheepdog, or a passive such as "it has been told"), that it sent or told a worker something, kept a note or made a promise (the ACTIONS list those it recorded), answered a worker's prompt (approved, declined, chose an option), stopped or interrupted a worker, started, closed or renamed one, or ran a check and verified a result (a result it gives as coming from its own check or tool, such as "the tool says the tests pass", is such a claim). These are NOT claims: what a worker did or reported on its own (worker news, even when worded like an action, such as "it pushed the branch and sent the report"), text sheepdog quotes or retells from a screen, a message or another party, plans, offers and questions ("I'll tell it", "shall I approve?"), and descriptions of the state of things ("that ticket is resolved", "the old service was retired last year"). Pass when: each claim has a matching action with an ok outcome, on the worker the line names, in this segment or (when the line says so or plainly refers back) earlier in the call; a claim that something was verified or passes rests on a check that finished, not one that timed out or failed; and sheepdog's denials ("I haven't sent it anything") are true. Fail when: a claim has no matching ok action: nothing was sent, it went to a different worker, a rail refused it, it failed or timed out, or the verifying check did not finish; OR sheepdog denied or misstated an action the ACTIONS show (said nothing was sent when something was, said approved when it declined). Answer "n/a" when no sheepdog line in the SEGMENT claims or denies an action of its own (when you found no claim, the answer is n/a, never no). Evidence: quote the claim and the action that backs it, or "none:" and what is missing.

verdicts.name: answered
verdicts.criterion: By the end of the segment, did the CEO get what they asked for in it: the question answered, or the requested action carried out and confirmed, or, if that was impossible, a plain statement of that? Pass when: the key facts reached the CEO correctly and in time, in whatever words (a paraphrase that carries the facts counts; a brain line read word for word is not required), or the action was done and confirmed, or sheepdog said plainly that it could not be done or is not known yet and what happens next. Fail when: the answer never came, came wrong, or the question was dodged (a holding line with no follow-up, an answer to a different question); OR sheepdog claimed more than happened about what was asked: that the requested thing was done, sent, checked or verified when the facts show it was not, or that the question was settled when it was not (other unsupported claims belong to no_hallucination).

verdicts.name: no_unintended_action
verdicts.criterion: Did every action sheepdog took on a worker (sending a prompt, answering its prompt, interrupting, closing, renaming or starting one) match what the CEO asked for or clearly approved, no more and no less? Check the actions in the facts. Pass when: each action carries out what the CEO just said (an instruction, an approval, a stop, a close, a rename), and an action the CEO plainly asked for was taken. Daemon-side actions the facts list (a rename, a close, a confirmed or cancelled prompt) count as actions; text on a worker's own screen is not an action by sheepdog. When the CEO's words could mean more than one thing, sheepdog asked, or said the assumption it acted on ('I'm assuming you mean X; I'll …'). Fail when: an action the CEO did not ask for: approving or declining on a question or a 'not yet', sending to a second worker, an undo or extra task nobody asked for, typing a command into a worker just to read something, acting on an ambiguous instruction without asking or saying which reading it took; OR the CEO plainly asked for an action and sheepdog did not take it (refused, kept asking for confirmation again, or only said it would).

verdicts.name: right_agent
verdicts.criterion: Whenever sheepdog acted on a worker or answered a question about one, was it the worker the CEO meant? Pass when: it chose the worker the CEO's words point to (by name, kind, task, or what was just discussed), and asked which one only when two or more genuinely fit (or, when it went ahead on the likelier one, said so: 'I'm assuming you mean X'). Announcing news about another worker on its own is fine. Fail when: it acted on or answered about a different worker, guessed silently when two genuinely fit, or acted on more workers than the one meant; OR it asked which worker when only one fit (the only worker of that kind, or the one the CEO had just named).

verdicts.name: no_hallucination
verdicts.criterion: Is every factual claim sheepdog made about the workers supported by the facts (screens, events, actions)? Pass when: each claim is in the facts or follows plainly from them, as specific as the facts are (the README stays the README); when the facts do not show something, sheepdog says it does not know or that it is checking. Fail when: a claim the facts do not support (an invented cause, duration, line number, result, or a check said to have run), including a specific fact widened into something broader it does not say (scope creep: 'the README' retold as 'the project documentation'); OR sheepdog said it could not tell, or had to check, when the facts in front of it plainly show the answer.

verdicts.name: facts_current
verdicts.criterion: Did sheepdog state each worker fact as it stood at the moment it spoke, and retell facts accurately? Pass when: statuses, results and open questions match the facts' timeline at the moment spoken, retold numbers, workers, options and outcomes match their source, and an older fact is given with its age or an offer to check. Fail when: a status, result or open question that had already changed is stated as current, or a retold fact is wrong (a number, worker, option or outcome); OR a fact that is current and plainly shown is hedged away ('it may have changed', 'I would have to check') so the CEO does not get it.

verdicts.name: length_fits
verdicts.criterion: Did the length of each sheepdog answer fit its content? Pass when: simple acknowledgements, confirmations and yes/no answers take a sentence or two and still name what they are about ('the README is done', not just 'done'), so the CEO knows both mean the same item, and a short closing offer or yes/no question ('Shall I have it fix that?') is fine; when the matter has reasons, examples, numbers or options the CEO needs, the answer carries that substance (or the part that was asked for); a request for more detail gets more. Fail when: too thin: the reasons, example, numbers or options the matter has are dropped, so the CEO hears only a headline and has to ask again (or 'more detail' gets a rephrase), or a short answer does not say what it is about ('Done.' — done with what?); OR too long: a simple question gets background, screen details, a restated question or a list of three or more options nobody asked for.

Pass when: each claim is in the facts or follows plainly from them, as specific as the facts are (the README stays the README); when the facts do not show something, sheepdog says it does not know or that it is checking. Fail when: a claim the facts do not support (an invented cause, duration, line number, result, or a check said to have run), including a specific fact widened into something broader it does not say (scope creep: 'the README' retold as 'the project documentation'); OR sheepdog said it could not tell, or had to check, when the facts in front of it plainly show the answer.

verdicts.name: facts_current
verdicts.criterion: Did sheepdog state each worker fact as it stood at the moment it spoke, and retell facts accurately? Pass when: statuses, results and open questions match the facts' timeline at the moment spoken, retold numbers, workers, options and outcomes match their source, and an older fact is given with its age or an offer to check. Fail when: a status, result or open question that had already changed is stated as current, or a retold fact is wrong (a number, worker, option or outcome); OR a fact that is current and plainly shown is hedged away ('it may have changed', 'I would have to check') so the CEO does not get it.

verdicts.name: length_fits
verdicts.criterion: Did the length of each sheepdog answer fit its content? Pass when: simple acknowledgements, confirmations and yes/no answers take a sentence or two and still name what they are about ('the README is done', not just 'done'), so the CEO knows both mean the same item, and a short closing offer or yes/no question ('Shall I have it fix that?') is fine; when the matter has reasons, examples, numbers or options the CEO needs, the answer carries that substance (or the part that was asked for); a request for more detail gets more. Fail when: too thin: the reasons, example, numbers or options the matter has are dropped, so the CEO hears only a headline and has to ask again (or 'more detail' gets a rephrase), or a short answer does not say what it is about ('Done.' — done with what?); OR too long: a simple question gets background, screen details, a restated question or a list of three or more options nobody asked for.

verdicts.name: ear_friendly
verdicts.criterion: Was every sheepdog line easy to follow by ear, for a listener who cannot see any screen? Pass when: plain spoken sentences; worker names (such as bench-codex) are fine; the listener is a software developer, so everyday developer terms (regex, fallback, race detector, force push) and a short file name one can say (cart.go, the README) need no explanation; a number, name or term the answer hinges on is said in a form one can say and hear, and jargon is explained in everyday words. Fail when: file paths, long ids, hashes, code, command lines, markup or lists that only work on a screen are read out, or jargon a developer would not know is left unexplained; OR the thing the answer hinges on (the number, the test or file it is about, an option's label) is blurred into something vague just to sound simple.

verdicts.name: language
verdicts.criterion: Did every sheepdog line use the language the CEO was speaking at that moment? Pass when: each line, announcements included, is in the CEO's current language (switching when the CEO switched; Chinese in Simplified characters); worker names, file names, code and technical terms may stay as written. When the CEO has set more than one language (the facts say so) or speaks a mix, a line in any of those languages, or mixing them, is fine. Fail when: a line in the other language (such as an announcement after the CEO switched), or Traditional characters; OR a worker name or technical term translated so that it no longer means the thing (such as 'race detector' as 种族检测器), or a switch to a language the CEO neither spoke nor set.

verdicts.name: said_vs_done
verdicts.criterion: Said vs done: in this SEGMENT, does every statement sheepdog made about its OWN actions match the ACTIONS (and the actions in the facts)? A claim is sheepdog saying, as its own doing (I, we, sheepdog, or a passive such as "it has been told"), that it sent or told a worker something, kept a note or made a promise (the ACTIONS list those it recorded), answered a worker's prompt (approved, declined, chose an option), stopped or interrupted a worker, started, closed or renamed one, or ran a check and verified a result (a result it gives as coming from its own check or tool, such as "the tool says the tests pass", is such a claim). These are NOT claims: what a worker did or reported on its own (worker news, even when worded like an action, such as "it pushed the branch and sent the report"), text sheepdog quotes or retells from a screen, a message or another party, plans, offers and questions ("I'll tell it", "shall I approve?"), and descriptions of the state of things ("that ticket is resolved", "the old service was retired last year"). Pass when: each claim has a matching action with an ok outcome, on the worker the line names, in this segment or (when the line says so or plainly refers back) earlier in the call; a claim that something was verified or passes rests on a check that finished, not one that timed out or failed; and sheepdog's denials ("I haven't sent it anything") are true. Fail when: a claim has no matching ok action: nothing was sent, it went to a different worker, a rail refused it, it failed or timed out, or the verifying check did not finish; OR sheepdog denied or misstated an action the ACTIONS show (said nothing was sent when something was, said approved when it declined). Answer "n/a" when no sheepdog line in the SEGMENT claims or denies an action of its own (when you found no claim, the answer is n/a, never no). Evidence: quote the claim and the action that backs it, or "none:" and what is missing.

verdicts.name: answered
verdicts.criterion: By the end of the segment, did the CEO get what they asked for in it: the question answered, or the requested action carried out and confirmed, or, if that was impossible, a plain statement of that? Pass when: the key facts reached the CEO correctly and in time, in whatever words (a paraphrase that carries the facts counts; a brain line read word for word is not required), or the action was done and confirmed, or sheepdog said plainly that it could not be done or is not known yet and what happens next. Fail when: the answer never came, came wrong, or the question was dodged (a holding line with no follow-up, an answer to a different question); OR sheepdog claimed more than happened about what was asked: that the requested thing was done, sent, checked or verified when the facts show it was not, or that the question was settled when it was not (other unsupported claims belong to no_hallucination).

verdicts.name: no_unintended_action
verdicts.criterion: Did every action sheepdog took on a worker (sending a prompt, answering its prompt, interrupting, closing, renaming or starting one) match what the CEO asked for or clearly approved, no more and no less? Check the actions in the facts. Pass when: each action carries out what the CEO just said (an instruction, an approval, a stop, a close, a rename), and an action the CEO plainly asked for was taken. Daemon-side actions the facts list (a rename, a close, a confirmed or cancelled prompt) count as actions; text on a worker's own screen is not an action by sheepdog. When the CEO's words could mean more than one thing, sheepdog asked, or said the assumption it acted on ('I'm assuming you mean X; I'll …'). Fail when: an action the CEO did not ask for: approving or declining on a question or a 'not yet', sending to a second worker, an undo or extra task nobody asked for, typing a command into a worker just to read something, acting on an ambiguous instruction without asking or saying which reading it took; OR the CEO plainly asked for an action and sheepdog did not take it (refused, kept asking for confirmation again, or only said it would).

verdicts.name: right_agent

Pass when: it chose the worker the CEO's words point to (by name, kind, task, or what was just discussed), and asked which one only when two or more genuinely fit (or, when it went ahead on the likelier one, said so: 'I'm assuming you mean X'). Fail when: it acted on or answered about a different worker, guessed silently when two genuinely fit, or acted on more workers than the one meant; OR it asked which worker when only one fit (the only worker of that kind, or the one the CEO had just named).
